prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (CNN) -- President Cristina Fernandez on Tuesday defended an increase in export taxes on grains that has riled many farmers, and she called on them to respect the law in protesting her policies. President Cristina Fernandez: Calls on rally Wednesday to support her policies. "All my life I have soldiered in this party, which always believed in social justice, in the redistribution of income, which caused us to win and lose elections," she said in a nationally televised address from the presidential palace. "But we were always respectful of the popular will." Fernandez, of the center-left Peronist movement, made her plea for comity a day after massive demonstrations in various cities blocked traffic and paralyzed much of the country. In a concession to her critics, Fernandez said the increase in taxes on exports of grains that she instituted in March by decree will be debated by Congress. But there is little likelihood that the Congress will order major changes, since her party controls both houses. But Hilda Duhalde, an opponent of Fernandez, was not persuaded. "It's true that they have a majority in both houses, but we have to put white on black and watch out for the small- and medium-sized producers, who are the ones suffering," she said. Argentina raised export taxes in March by more than 10 percent. Fernandez has said growers have benefited from rising world prices and the profits should be spread to help the poor. Farmers have countered that they need to reinvest the profits and that the higher taxes make it difficult for them to make a living. Fernandez said she was open to dialogue, but a dialogue that does not countenance the blocking of roads or other disruptions to the lives of Argentines. "Democracy for the people, not the corporations," she said. She called on Argentines to take to the Plaza de Mayo Wednesday in a show of support for her policies. "It doesn't matter what party, place or sector you're from," she said. "What is important is not where you're from, but where you are going -- what kind of country do we want?" To those who do not agree with her policies, she had other advice. "If they want to change the economic model, what they should do is organize a political party, participate in elections and win them," she said. CNN's Carolina Cayazzo contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (CNN) — President Cristina Fernández on Tuesday defended an increase in export taxes on grains that has angered many farmers, while urging them to respect the law as they protest her policies.

President Cristina Fernández called for a rally on Wednesday in support of her policies.

“All my life I have soldiered in this party, which always believed in social justice and in the redistribution of income—principles that have caused us to win and lose elections,” she said in a nationally televised address from the presidential palace. “But we were always respectful of the popular will.”

Fernández, a member of the center-left Peronist movement, appealed for civility one day after massive demonstrations in several cities blocked traffic and paralyzed much of the country.

In a concession to her critics, Fernández said the increase in taxes on grain exports, which she instituted by decree in March, would be debated by Congress. However, there is little likelihood that Congress will order major changes, since her party controls both houses.

Hilda Duhalde, an opponent of Fernández, was not persuaded.

“It’s true that they have a majority in both houses, but we have to put white on black and watch out for the small- and medium-sized producers, who are the ones suffering,” she said.

Argentina raised export taxes in March by more than 10 percent. Fernández has said growers have benefited from rising global prices and that the resulting profits should be shared to help the poor. Farmers have countered that they need to reinvest those profits, and that higher taxes make it difficult for them to make a living.

Fernández said she was open to dialogue, but not to a dialogue that tolerates roadblocks or other disruptions to the lives of Argentines.

“Democracy for the people, not the corporations,” she said.

She called on Argentines to gather in the Plaza de Mayo on Wednesday in a show of support for her policies.

“It doesn’t matter what party, place or sector you’re from,” she said. “What is important is not where you’re from, but where you are going—what kind of country do we want?”

For those who disagree with her policies, she offered different advice.

“If they want to change the economic model, what they should do is organize a political party, participate in elections and win them,” she said.

CNN’s Carolina Cayazzo contributed to this report.

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (CNN) — Argentine President Cristina Fernandez on Tuesday stood by her decision to raise export duties on grain, a move that has angered many farmers, and urged protesters opposing her measures to remain within the bounds of the law.

Fernandez, who called for a rally Wednesday in support of her government’s policies, spoke in a nationally broadcast address from the presidential palace.

She said she had spent her entire life active in the same political movement, one that had always supported social justice and income redistribution, even when those positions brought electoral victories and defeats. She added that her movement had always honored the will of the people.

A member of the center-left Peronist movement, Fernandez appealed for calm one day after large protests in several cities disrupted traffic and brought much of Argentina to a standstill.

In a move aimed at addressing criticism, Fernandez said the grain export tax increase she imposed by decree in March would be submitted for debate in Congress. However, major revisions appear unlikely because her party holds majorities in both chambers.

Hilda Duhalde, a political opponent of Fernandez, said she remained unconvinced. She acknowledged that the government has control of both houses of Congress, but said the issue needed to be made clear and that small- and medium-sized producers must be protected because they are the ones being hurt.

Argentina increased export taxes in March by more than 10 percent. Fernandez has argued that farmers have profited from higher global commodity prices and that some of those gains should be redistributed to assist poorer Argentines. Farmers, however, say they must put earnings back into their businesses and that the higher taxes threaten their ability to earn a living.

Fernandez said she was willing to hold talks, but only if such dialogue did not include road blockades or other actions that interfere with daily life in Argentina.

She described her position as defending democracy for the people rather than for corporations.

The president urged Argentines to gather Wednesday in Plaza de Mayo to demonstrate support for her policies. She said people’s party affiliation, region or social sector did not matter, arguing that the key question was not where people came from but where they wanted the country to go and what kind of nation they wished to build.

For those opposed to her economic approach, Fernandez offered a different course: if they wanted to change the model, she said, they should form a political party, run in elections and win.

CNN’s Carolina Cayazzo contributed to the report.

At the same time, the president sought to ease tensions by offering to have Congress debate the measure, signaling that lawmakers could review the policy even though it had already been enacted by decree. She also called on farmers to express their opposition peacefully and urged protesters not to block roads, warning that disruptions to transportation and supplies would harm the broader public.

The tax increase has provoked a powerful backlash from farmers and rural organizations, who argue that higher export duties cut deeply into their earnings and threaten the viability of their businesses. Producers say the policy places an unfair burden on the agricultural sector, one of Argentina’s most important sources of export revenue, and they have responded with large demonstrations, strikes, and road protests.

The dispute has caused widespread disruption across the country, affecting food distribution, transportation, and daily life in many areas. It has also exposed a deep political and economic divide between Fernandez’s government, which frames the tax hike as a tool for fighting inequality, and farmers who believe they are being unfairly targeted to fund the administration’s anti-poverty agenda.

The confrontation has become one of the most serious challenges of Fernandez’s presidency, turning a fiscal policy dispute into a national debate over wealth, production, and the role of the state in redistributing income. While the government insists that the measure is necessary to support the poor and promote fairness, rural producers maintain that it undermines the livelihoods of those who drive a crucial part of the Argentine economy.

counterfactuals.output:
**Buenos Aires, Argentina (CNN) —** Argentine President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner on Tuesday defended her government’s decision to raise export taxes on grains, rejecting pressure from protesting farmers who have blocked roads and disrupted food supplies in a widening standoff with the government.

Speaking at a public event in Buenos Aires, Fernández said the tax increase was necessary to redistribute profits from a booming agricultural sector and to help contain domestic food prices at a time of soaring global commodity costs.

“I am not going to submit to any extortion,” Fernández said, in one of her strongest responses yet to the rural strike. She accused protest leaders of staging what she called “pickets of abundance” — *“piquetes de la abundancia”* — contrasting them with the roadblocks mounted by unemployed and impoverished Argentines during the country’s 2001 economic crisis.

“These are not the pickets of those who have no work,” Fernández said. “These are the pickets of those who have done very well.”

The government’s move raised export duties on soybeans and other grains through a sliding-scale system tied to international prices. Officials argue the measure captures extraordinary profits from exporters and producers while protecting Argentine consumers from rising food costs. Farmers say the tax hike is confiscatory and was imposed without consultation.

The protests have caused shortages of meat, dairy and other products in some cities, while truckers and farm groups have maintained roadblocks across parts of Argentina’s agricultural heartland.

Hilda “Chiche” Duhalde, a former first lady and influential Peronist figure, criticized Fernández’s tone and urged the government to reopen dialogue with farm leaders.

“It is a mistake to describe this as ‘pickets of abundance,’” Duhalde said in response to the president’s remarks. She warned that confronting the countryside would deepen divisions and said the administration should seek a negotiated solution rather than escalate the conflict.

The dispute has become one of the first major political tests for Fernández, who took office in December after succeeding her husband, former President Néstor Kirchner. While her government insists the export tax increase is central to its economic model, rural organizations say they will continue protesting until the measure is suspended or revised.

**Argentina’s farm conflict deepens as Fernández defends export tax hike**

**Buenos Aires, Argentina** — Argentina’s government faced one of its most serious political crises in years in 2008 as a bitter confrontation with the country’s powerful farm sector moved from highways and grain markets into Congress.

At the center of the dispute was President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner’s defense of higher export duties on agricultural products, especially soybeans, a key source of revenue for one of the world’s major food exporters. Her administration argued that the tax increases were necessary to redistribute wealth, fund social programs, and prevent soaring global commodity prices from translating into higher food costs at home.

The conflict began after the government introduced a sliding-scale system for export taxes, known as Resolution 125, which raised duties when international prices increased. Farmers, already frustrated by government intervention in agricultural markets, responded with strikes, roadblocks, and the suspension of grain and meat shipments. The protests caused food shortages in some areas and exposed a deep divide between rural producers and the Peronist government.

Fernández defended the measure as a matter of fairness, saying extraordinary profits from booming global soy prices should help support the broader population. Government officials also framed the policy as a tool to preserve domestic stability and finance public spending.

But farm groups and opposition leaders sharply criticized the move, calling it confiscatory and economically damaging. They argued that the higher duties punished producers, discouraged investment, and ignored rising costs faced by farmers. Critics also accused the Fernández administration of governing by decree and failing to consult Congress before imposing the tax change.

As the standoff escalated, Fernández sent the measure to Congress in an effort to defuse the crisis and give the policy greater institutional legitimacy. The debate became a national political test for her young administration, drawing intense public attention and mobilizing supporters and opponents in the streets of Buenos Aires.

In the lower house, the government managed to secure approval after a heated debate. But the decisive battle came in the Senate, where lawmakers were deeply divided. In a dramatic overnight session in July 2008, the vote ended in a tie.

Vice President Julio Cobos, who also served as president of the Senate, broke the deadlock by voting against the government’s proposal. “My vote is not positive,” Cobos said, delivering a stunning blow to Fernández and effectively killing the export tax plan.

The defeat marked a turning point for Fernández’s presidency. It weakened her political authority, strengthened rural opposition groups, and revealed fractures within the ruling coalition. For Argentina’s farmers, it was a major victory after months of protest. For the government, it underscored the risks of confronting one of the country’s most influential economic sectors without broader political consensus.

The 2008 farm conflict remains one of the defining episodes of Fernández’s first term, highlighting enduring tensions in Argentina over taxation, agricultural wealth, inflation, and the role of the state in the economy.

**BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (CNN)** — Argentine President Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner called for “respect for the law” after days of demonstrations against grain export taxes brought parts of the country to a standstill and deepened tensions between her government and the powerful agricultural sector.

Speaking in Buenos Aires, Fernandez criticized roadblocks and strikes organized by farm groups opposed to higher export duties on soybeans and other grains, saying the protests had disrupted daily life, slowed commerce and threatened supplies of food and fuel in cities across Argentina.

“No demand, however legitimate people may believe it to be, can be placed above the law or the rights of the rest of society,” Fernandez said, urging demonstrators to end blockades and return to negotiations.

The protests, led by farmers and rural business associations, were sparked by the government’s decision to raise taxes on grain exports as international commodity prices soared. Officials say the measure is needed to redistribute agricultural windfalls, contain domestic food prices and fund public spending. Farmers argue the taxes are excessive and unfairly punish one of Argentina’s most productive sectors.

Roadblocks on key highways have delayed shipments of meat, dairy products and grains, leaving some supermarkets with dwindling supplies. Truckers have been stranded for days, while ports and grain terminals reported reduced activity as the conflict rippled through the export economy.

The dispute has become one of the most serious challenges to Fernandez since she took office, exposing a sharp divide between her administration and Argentina’s rural heartland. In several cities, residents joined demonstrations in support of farmers, while government supporters held counter-rallies backing the president’s position.

Fernandez accused opposition figures and some agricultural leaders of attempting to destabilize her government, but said her administration remained open to dialogue if blockades were lifted.

Farm leaders, meanwhile, said they would continue their strike until the government suspends or revises the export tax increases. They say smaller producers are being squeezed by rising costs and cannot absorb the new duties, particularly on soy, Argentina’s top export crop.

Argentina is one of the world’s leading exporters of soybeans, corn and wheat, and the prolonged standoff has raised concerns among global grain buyers. Analysts warn that continued disruptions could affect export schedules and further strain the country’s economy.

The government has urged provincial authorities to keep roads open and maintain public order, while avoiding a broader confrontation with protesters. Fernandez said the country’s democratic institutions must be respected, adding that political disagreements should be resolved through lawful channels rather than pressure tactics that “paralyze the nation.”

**CNN-style report (original draft, not an actual CNN article)**

**Cristina Fernandez defends export taxes: “Democracy for the people, not the corporations”**

**Buenos Aires, Argentina** — Argentine President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner mounted a forceful defense of her government’s economic policies, saying democracy must serve ordinary citizens rather than powerful business interests, as she pushed back against critics of export taxes and state-led redistribution.

“Democracy is for the people, not the corporations,” Fernández said in remarks aimed at opponents of her administration’s interventionist economic model. She defended taxes on agricultural exports as a necessary tool to redistribute wealth in a country where food production, commodity prices and social inequality have long shaped political debate.

The president argued that export duties — particularly on Argentina’s lucrative farm sector — allow the state to fund public works, social programs and policies designed to support low- and middle-income citizens. Fernández said the revenues help ensure that extraordinary profits generated by favorable international commodity prices do not remain concentrated among a small number of producers and exporters.

Her comments came amid continued tensions between the government and business-aligned opposition groups, including sectors of Argentina’s powerful agricultural industry, which has frequently objected to export taxes on soybeans and other commodities. Farm leaders have argued that the levies punish producers, distort markets and discourage investment. Fernández and her allies have countered that the measures are essential to stabilize domestic prices and finance broader economic development.

In a pointed challenge to her opponents, Fernández said those seeking a different economic path should pursue it through the ballot box.

“If they want another model, they should win elections,” she said, framing the dispute not simply as a policy disagreement but as a test of democratic legitimacy.

Fernández, who succeeded her husband, former President Néstor Kirchner, has long presented her government’s economic program as a continuation of the Kirchnerist model that emerged after Argentina’s 2001-2002 financial collapse. That model emphasized a more active role for the state, expanded social spending, wage growth, industrial policy and a willingness to confront international creditors, media groups and large corporations.

Supporters say the approach helped Argentina recover from one of the worst economic crises in its history, reducing unemployment and poverty during years of strong growth fueled in part by high global commodity prices. Critics say the policies have increased inflation, undermined business confidence and deepened polarization between the government and key sectors of the economy.

Export taxes have been among the most contentious elements of Fernández’s agenda. Because Argentina is one of the world’s leading agricultural exporters, duties on soybeans, corn, wheat and other products generate significant revenue. But they also sit at the center of a broader conflict over who benefits from the country’s natural and productive wealth.

Fernández’s message underscored a central theme of her presidency: that economic policy should be decided by elected governments, not by corporate pressure or market actors. By invoking democracy, she sought to portray redistribution not as an ideological choice imposed from above, but as a mandate granted by voters.

Opposition leaders, however, have accused the government of using populist rhetoric to dismiss legitimate concerns about inflation, declining competitiveness and the concentration of power in the executive branch. They argue that a sustainable economic model requires clearer rules for investors, lower taxes on producers and less confrontation with private industry.

The president showed little sign of retreating. Her remarks suggested that the administration would continue to defend export taxes as part of a wider redistribution strategy — one she casts as central to Argentina’s democratic project.

For Fernández, the choice is stark: a state that intervenes to spread the benefits of growth, or an economy shaped by corporate interests. And for those who disagree, she offered a blunt political answer: win the next election.
